virals.name: Larry Augustin
virals.text:
When someone says they vibe coded their own CRM over a weekend, I believe the part about the weekend. I spent years running SugarCRM. With a CRM, the hard part starts on Monday.

A weekend build shows the software can work once, with inputs the builder expected. The company needs it working in month six, when a login token expires, the builder is on vacation, and a customer asks who can see their data.

Fred Brooks estimated in 1975 that a program anybody can run, repair, and connect to other systems costs nine times as much as one that runs for its author. Vibe coding made the author's version nearly free. The other eight-ninths of the bill comes due later.

New Relic commissioned a 2026 survey of 200 US technology leaders. In code review, 94% rated AI-generated code higher quality than code people wrote. Over the prior six months, 82% reported at least one production failure tied to AI-generated code.

A vibe-coded CRM has exactly one throat to choke, and it belongs to whoever wrote the prompts. When that person moves on, the company's customer records have no owner.

I run about 20 AI agents. They're baling wire. The connection that tells my system I've sent an email quietly died more than a month before a watchdog agent noticed.

Making my fleet a real application would take error reporting, security, compliance, and everything else a business depends on.

An application is a promise that someone will still be there to fix it in month six.

Full article in the reply.

virals.text:
Still a work in progress, but I've been experimenting with something called VibeCodeFolks. And it started with a question:

AI can write 1,000 lines of code before you finish your coffee.

But can you explain those 1,000 lines?

I've been seeing senior engineers and engineering managers discuss how vibe coding is making code reviews harder, not easier.

We've made writing code ridiculously cheap. But understanding, debugging, and maintaining it? Not so much.

An AI agent can modify your frontend, backend, APIs, and infrastructure in one session.

Git tells you WHAT changed. Understanding WHY, HOW the pieces connect, and WHERE things might break is still on you.

So I'm building VibeCodeFolks, an open-source, local-first CLI in Go.

Run vibecodefolks . after an AI coding session. It attempts to:

Explain changes with actual code references.
Visualize how affected components might connect.
Quiz you on the code AI just wrote.

And the quiz is the part I'm most interested in.

Getting a question wrong won't block you from shipping. It's not a certification or a correctness check.

But if I struggle to answer questions about a change, I'd probably want to understand that part better before shipping it.

Sometimes the most useful thing a tool can do isn't give you another answer. It's help you realize what you don't understand yet.

Now, the obvious counterargument: isn't this just spending MORE AI tokens to understand AI-generated code?

Fair point.

But anyone who's vibe coded long enough probably knows this loop:

"Fix this bug."
"Now something else broke."
"Try again."
More prompts. More tokens. More time.
I wonder if spending a few extra tokens understanding changes upfront could sometimes be cheaper than debugging something you never understood.

It's still an early experiment. The explanations, visualizations, and quizzes need improvement, and I haven't established whether this approach actually saves time or tokens.

But it raises an interesting question:

Are we getting better at building software, or just faster at generating code we don't fully understand?

Curious how other engineers and teams are handling vibe coding at their orgs

THIS IS PURE F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic just quietly shipped one of the strongest setups for Claude Code

The idea: make Opus 5.5 the team lead, and let cheap Haiku 5.5 teammates swarm the work in parallel

Opus-grade planning on every task, without paying Opus to babysit a hundred routine turns

You just launch Claude Code like this:

export CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1
claude --model opus --teammate-mode auto

here's the split:

→ Opus 5.5 leads the team, turns your goal into a task DAG, and signs off at the end
→ Haiku 5.5 teammates self-claim unblocked tasks, each in its own isolated context
→ Sonnet 5.5 takes the heavy multi-file patches without blocking anyone else
→ teammates talk to each other over a P2P mailbox, so Opus never reads the chatter

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ locking the dependency DAG before anyone starts
→ approving the diff plan before a teammate touches code
→ signing off on verified results before anything ships

Opus leads · Haiku claims · Sonnet patches

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which teammate, retry or stop) clear through JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that actually split

> Opus 5.5 runs the lead session and owns the task DAG
> security audits auth and JWT handling on Haiku 5.5
> perf-scout hunts p99 latency bottlenecks on Haiku 5.5
> qa-engine runs the full test suite on Haiku 5.5
> patcher lands multi-file fixes on Sonnet 5.5 once its blockers clear
> teammates hand off findings through the P2P mailbox
> Opus 5.5 reads only the verified PR diff
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

Anthropic Engineering Lead Felix Rieseberg revealed how they monitor Claude Code in production

before Fable drops, multi-agent runs on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 hide a lethal loop that burns entire token budgets in silence

the fix is not more logs, it is this single flag:

export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1

why naive agent clusters crash and burn budget:
- 40,000-line flat terminal logs hide which subagent hallucinated invalid state
- recursive retry loops burn hundreds of dollars on unmonitored failures
- zero cache visibility hides whether prompts hit prefix cache or re-tokenize

Anthropic solved this with their official telemetry guide: anthropics/claude-code-monitoring-guide

the architecture replaces blind console dumps with distributed OpenTelemetry trace DAGs:

1. W3C Distributed Trace Context
every agent session generates a root trace ID with typed child spans
planning spans, tool execution spans, and subagent forks track exact causal parentage
isolate root failures in milliseconds instead of grepping flat stdout

2. Prefix-Cache Telemetry
Prometheus tracks claude_code_token_usage by cacheRead and cacheCreation
monitor 90%+ prompt cache hit ratios in real time across Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5
stop paying frontier token prices on static system instructions

3. Automated Circuit Breakers
detect unmonitored retry spirals before token budgets explode
OTel collector halts execution the second an agent triggers an identical error loop
zero recursive token burn, deterministic spend caps, and instant alert routing

4. Real-Time Prometheus Cost Meters
claude_code_cost_usage streams cost per session, per model, and per tool
track exact ROI per bug fix and feature commit directly inside Prometheus and Grafana

- alert on recursive retry loops exceeding 3 identical tool errors

- Builder agent on Sonnet 5.5: trace code generation and test execution spans
- Evaluator agent on Opus 5.5: trace independent review and rubric validation

outsiders.name: Larry Augustin
outsiders.text:
When someone says they vibe coded their own CRM over a weekend, I believe the part about the weekend. I spent years running SugarCRM. With a CRM, the hard part starts on Monday.

A weekend build shows the software can work once, with inputs the builder expected. The company needs it working in month six, when a login token expires, the builder is on vacation, and a customer asks who can see their data.

Fred Brooks estimated in 1975 that a program anybody can run, repair, and connect to other systems costs nine times as much as one that runs for its author. Vibe coding made the author's version nearly free. The other eight-ninths of the bill comes due later.

New Relic commissioned a 2026 survey of 200 US technology leaders. In code review, 94% rated AI-generated code higher quality than code people wrote. Over the prior six months, 82% reported at least one production failure tied to AI-generated code.

A vibe-coded CRM has exactly one throat to choke, and it belongs to whoever wrote the prompts. When that person moves on, the company's customer records have no owner.

I run about 20 AI agents. They're baling wire. The connection that tells my system I've sent an email quietly died more than a month before a watchdog agent noticed.

Making my fleet a real application would take error reporting, security, compliance, and everything else a business depends on.

An application is a promise that someone will still be there to fix it in month six.

Full article in the reply.

outsiders.text:
THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku and Opus 5.5 together, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Opus-level judgment on every big call, without paying Opus rates for every routine turn.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session and writes the code
→ Haiku 5.5 explores files and docs in parallel
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls
→ you stop spending Opus on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku explores. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and edits code
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5
> docs pulls the API reference on Haiku 5.5
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reads the whole transcript when consulted
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

Still a work in progress, but I've been experimenting with something called VibeCodeFolks. And it started with a question:

AI can write 1,000 lines of code before you finish your coffee.

But can you explain those 1,000 lines?

I've been seeing senior engineers and engineering managers discuss how vibe coding is making code reviews harder, not easier.

We've made writing code ridiculously cheap. But understanding, debugging, and maintaining it? Not so much.

An AI agent can modify your frontend, backend, APIs, and infrastructure in one session.

Git tells you WHAT changed. Understanding WHY, HOW the pieces connect, and WHERE things might break is still on you.

So I'm building VibeCodeFolks, an open-source, local-first CLI in Go.

Run vibecodefolks . after an AI coding session. It attempts to:

Explain changes with actual code references.
Visualize how affected components might connect.
Quiz you on the code AI just wrote.

And the quiz is the part I'm most interested in.

Getting a question wrong won't block you from shipping. It's not a certification or a correctness check.

But if I struggle to answer questions about a change, I'd probably want to understand that part better before shipping it.

Sometimes the most useful thing a tool can do isn't give you another answer. It's help you realize what you don't understand yet.

Now, the obvious counterargument: isn't this just spending MORE AI tokens to understand AI-generated code?

Fair point.

But anyone who's vibe coded long enough probably knows this loop:

"Fix this bug."
"Now something else broke."
"Try again."
More prompts. More tokens. More time.
I wonder if spending a few extra tokens understanding changes upfront could sometimes be cheaper than debugging something you never understood.

It's still an early experiment. The explanations, visualizations, and quizzes need improvement, and I haven't established whether this approach actually saves time or tokens.

But it raises an interesting question:

Are we getting better at building software, or just faster at generating code we don't fully understand?

Curious how other engineers and teams are handling vibe coding at their orgs
